declarations.description:
Closes an overlay on Escape or on a pointer press outside it.

Both, because they are different intentions with the same meaning: Escape is
the keyboard's way out and clicking away is the pointer's, and an overlay
that honours only one is one half its readers cannot dismiss.

The outside press is watched on `pointerdown` rather than `click`, so a press
that starts outside and drags across the overlay still counts as leaving
rather than as interacting.

A press inside a frame is the third case, and it needs its own signal. The
frame swallows the event, so the document that owns the overlay never sees a
`pointerdown` at all, and where the frame is cross-origin there is nothing to
listen to inside it either. What is observable is that the window lost focus
and a frame on this page gained it, which is exactly a press the document
cannot see. Leaving the browser altogether blurs the window too, so what took
focus is the part that distinguishes them.
declarations.name: DismissController

members.name: handleWindowBlur
members.description:
Focus left the document. If a frame took it, that was a press.

Deferred by a task, because the order of `blur` against the focus moving is
not something every browser agrees on and reading `activeElement` too early
gives the element that is losing focus rather than the one taking it. The
guard is for the case where the overlay closed for another reason in
between, which would otherwise dismiss whatever opened next.

members.name: activate
members.description: Starts listening.

members.name: deactivate
members.description: Stops listening.

declarations.description:
Places one element against another, and keeps it there.

Positioning is `@floating-ui/dom` rather than arithmetic written here. Two
things in particular are why. A `position: fixed` element inside an ancestor
carrying `transform`, `filter`, `will-change`, or `contain` is positioned
against that ancestor and not the viewport, so viewport coordinates land it
somewhere else entirely. And an overlay has to clear its nearest *clipping*
ancestor, not just the window, or it is placed correctly inside a scrolling
panel and clipped out of sight by it. Both are ordinary here, and both are a
long tail of browser behaviour rather than a formula.

`autoUpdate` keeps the position through scrolling on any ancestor, resizes of
either element, and layout shifts.

The side the element actually landed on is written back as `data-placement`,
so a styled tier can animate from it rather than from the side that was
asked for.
declarations.name: FloatingController

members.description: The placement in use after the last measurement.

members.name: start
members.description: Starts placing, and keeps placing until stopped.

members.name: stop
members.description: Stops placing and releases everything it was tracking.

declarations.description:
Keeps Tab inside a container while it is open, and gives focus back after.

A dialog that does not trap focus is one a keyboard user tabs straight out
of, into a page they cannot see and cannot get back from. Restoring focus on
release matters just as much: without it, closing a drawer drops the reader
at the top of the document.

Finding the focusable elements is `focusableElements`, which is a utility
rather than part of this, because that half is what roving tabindex and
arrow-key navigation need and neither of them traps anything.
declarations.name: FocusTrapController

members.name: activate
members.description: Starts trapping, remembering where focus came from.

members.name: deactivate
members.description: Stops trapping and returns focus to wherever it was.

declarations.description:
Fired when an element is about to open.

Cancelable: `preventDefault()` refuses the change, and the element stays
closed. Paired with `helix-close` rather than being one event carrying a
boolean, so a listener that only cares about one direction says so by which
event it listens for.

Neither bubbles nor composed. A dialog inside a drawer inside a popover is
three overlays, and an inner one opening must not read as the outer one
opening.
declarations.name: HelixOpenEvent

declarations.description: Fired when an element is about to close. See `HelixOpenEvent`.
declarations.name: HelixCloseEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when an element asks to be taken away.

A request rather than a notification: the element does not remove itself,
because the consumer owns the markup it is in and removing the node under
them would put their state and the document out of step. Cancelable, so
`preventDefault()` is a refusal.

One verb for both shapes. A tag leaving a list and a banner closing itself
are the same act from the element's side.
declarations.name: HelixDismissEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when a value changes on something that is not a native input.

One hyphen, which is the limit of what React binds on a custom element.
`onhelix-change` reaches this; `onhelix-value-change`, which this was called,
reached nothing, because React stops at one hyphen and binds no event whose
name carries two.

The prefix is what keeps it clear of the native `change`. A consumer writes
`onhelix-change` for this and `onChange` for a real input's own, and the two
cannot be confused for each other. A control wrapping a native input relays
that input's `change` under its own name as well.
declarations.name: HelixChangeEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when something being previewed writes to the console.

Carries text rather than the logged values. The preview is a separate
document, so what arrives has crossed `postMessage` and been through
structured clone: a DOM node or a function does not survive that, and half a
value is worse than a string of it.
declarations.name: HelixConsoleEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the cursor moves in a text editor.

Not cancelable, unlike everything else here. The others announce something
about to happen and a listener can refuse it; this one reports where the
caret already is, and there is nothing left to refuse.

It fires on every keystroke and every arrow press, which is why the status
bar reads it from the DOM rather than through a framework's state: routing a
caret position through React would re-render the workbench on every cursor
move.
declarations.name: HelixCaretEvent

declarations.description:
Fired when the reader selects an item in a set.

Bubbles and is composed, because this is how a set coordinates: a tree, a
tab list and a toggle group all learn which of their children was chosen by
hearing it arrive.
declarations.name: HelixSelectEvent

declarations.description:
Owns only what is universal: normalizing `box-sizing` inside the shadow root,
so component CSS can rely on border-box on both sides of the boundary.

There is deliberately no `emit(name, detail)` helper. A dispatch through a
generic helper cannot be named by the manifest analyzer, which recorded the
parameter identifier and produced a phantom event on every element that
inherited it. Components dispatch concrete event classes from `events.ts`,
which the analyzer and TypeScript can both see.
declarations.name: HelixElement

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: Base class every Helix element extends.

declarations.description:
This has to be a class rather than a mixin or controller, and that is not a
style preference: the browser reads `formAssociated` off the constructor
during element upgrade, which cannot be delegated to a composed object.

`internals` comes from `HelixElement`, which attaches it for every component.
`attachInternals()` throws on a second call, so there is exactly one owner.

Deliberately small. It carries what every form participant needs and nothing
more; `value`, validity, and the reset and restore callbacks land when the
first input does, rather than being designed against components that do not
exist yet.

members.name: checked
members.description: Whether the control is checked. Setting this enters controlled mode.

members.name: defaultChecked
members.description: Initial checked state for uncontrolled use. Ignored once `checked` is set.

members.name: isChecked
members.description: The resolved checked state, whichever mode the element is in.

members.name: onCheckedChange
members.description:
The consumer's callback, invoked after the state is applied.

A React consumer cannot pass this through JSX: React reserves every prop
matching `on[A-Z]` and drops the ones it does not recognise. The generated
wrapper listens for `helix-change` instead. This is for a consumer
holding a reference, or a framework that assigns properties.

members.name: requestChecked
members.description:
Requests a checked change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts: a listener calling `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-change` refuses the change, and nothing moves.

members.name: toggleChecked
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: resetChecked
members.description:
Drops the uncontrolled state, so the control reads `defaultChecked` again.

A form reset has to return a control to what its markup declared. Clearing
`checked` alone cannot do it: that only leaves controlled mode, and the
uncontrolled value the element has been keeping is private to the mixin
and would still be what `isChecked` reports.

declarations.description:
Grafts controlled and uncontrolled checked state onto a base class.

Controlled mode is detected automatically: once a consumer sets `checked`,
the element stops managing the value and only announces. Uncontrolled
consumers set `defaultChecked` and let the element own it.

Sets `data-checked` on the host whenever the element is checked, in either
mode. Styled tiers select on that rather than `[checked]`, which is absent
for uncontrolled consumers.

declarations.description:
Grafts a label, help text, and a validation message onto a form control.

Every form control wants the same three things around it and wants them in a
different arrangement: a label above an input, beside a checkbox, and over a
group. So this owns the properties, the parts, and the wiring, and each
control places the nodes where its own geometry needs them. Same part names
either way, so one stylesheet in the styled tier dresses all of them.

**Not a wrapping `Field` component, and that is not a style preference.** A
wrapper cannot name what it wraps. Its label would live in its own shadow
root and the control in another, and measured in Chrome 148: an
`aria-labelledby` IDREF cannot see across, and
`control.ariaLabelledByElements = [labelInTheWrapper]` reads back as zero
elements, the reference dropped. The same assignment with a label in the
control's own tree is kept. That pattern works in React libraries because
they have no shadow boundary; bringing it here brings the ergonomics and none
of the conditions that made it work.

**A control whose label is its content renders its own.** A checkbox is named
by the words beside it, inside the `<label>` that forwards the press, so it
uses its default slot and nesting `renderLabel`'s `<label>` in there would be
invalid markup. `label` is that slot's fallback either way.

Worth knowing, because it costs a label and gives no warning: **a
whitespace-only text node is assigned to the default slot and defeats its
fallback.** Measured in Chrome 148, and a newline between the tags is enough,
so `<helix-checkbox label="Accept">` closed on the next line renders no label
at all. A named slot does not have this problem, because `slot="label"` is an
attribute and a text node has none. It is the platform's behaviour rather
than ours, and the same is already true of every slot fallback here.

**The ids are fixed rather than generated.** IDREFs resolve within the tree
that holds them, so two controls on a page each carrying `helix-hint` in
their own shadow root do not collide. That also removes the usual hydration
hazard, since there is no generated value for a server and a client to
disagree about.

**A group has to say it differently.** A control's `<input>` and its hint
are both in the shadow root, so a plain `aria-describedby` resolves. A
group's host is in the light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot
reach and `element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference. Only
`internals.ariaDescribedByElements` keeps it, which is what `describeHost`
uses. Measured the same way, and the failure is silent either way: the
description simply never reaches the accessibility tree.
declarations.name: MixinField

members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: hideLabel

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: resolvedFeedback
members.description: The message actually shown: the consumer's, or the platform's, or none.

members.name: describedBy
members.description:
Id of the description node, for `aria-describedby` on the control.

One at a time, because only one of the two is ever rendered. Naming both
would point a screen reader at an id that resolves to nothing, which it
reads as a description it cannot find.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

Naming a control without showing the label is `hide-label`, not an empty
one: an unnamed field is a field a screen reader announces as "edit text".

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

declarations.name: createSheet
declarations.description:
Builds a stylesheet from CSS authored in a `.css` file.

Component styles live in real `.css` files rather than `css` tagged
templates, so they get CSS tooling: syntax highlighting, formatters, the
token linter, and a diff that reads as CSS. `bun run styles` compiles each
one into a sibling `.css.ts` that calls this.

The `unsafe` in `unsafeCSS` warns about interpolating untrusted input into a
stylesheet. That is not what happens here: the argument is a build-time
constant read from a file in this repo, never a runtime value. Wrapping it
keeps the warning where it belongs, on `unsafeCSS` itself, and gives one seam
to change if constructable stylesheets become the better primitive.

declarations.name: customElement
declarations.description:
Registers a custom element, once.

A drop-in replacement for Lit's `@customElement` that does not throw when the
tag is already registered.

The duplicate is not hypothetical. Next.js evaluates a module in both the
server and client graphs, so a component imported by a server component and a
client component runs its registration twice against one registry, and
`customElements.define` throws:

> Failed to execute 'define': the name "helix-card" has already been used

That failure takes down the whole prerender, and it appears only once an app
mixes server and client usage of the same component, which is exactly what a
real app does.

The analyzer detects `@customElement` **by decorator name**, not by where it
is imported from, so the manifest still records `tagName` and nothing
downstream changes.

declarations.name: focusableElements
declarations.description:
Everything inside `root` the reader can reach with Tab, in document order.

Separate from the focus trap because finding is the half most callers want:
roving tabindex, arrow-key navigation and "focus the first thing" all need
this list and none of them traps anything.

Visibility is tested with `getClientRects()` rather than `offsetParent`,
which is null for anything inside a `position: fixed` container. A drawer is
exactly that, so the `offsetParent` test excluded every control in the thing
being trapped.

declarations.name: deepActiveElement
declarations.description:
The truly focused element, following shadow roots down.

`document.activeElement` stops at the outermost host, so a button inside two
shadow roots reports as the component rather than as itself.

declarations.name: requestControlledChange
declarations.description:
Announces a change, then applies it if nobody refused.

One audited path for every stateful change in the system. The order is the
whole point: the event goes first and carries the state being *proposed*, so
a listener calling `preventDefault()` stops it before anything moves. A
component that mutated itself and then announced it would leave a consumer
reacting to a decision already made.

Returns whether the change was applied, so a caller that needs to know
(a key handler deciding whether to also move focus) can ask.

A throwing `notify` is caught and logged rather than rethrown. A consumer's
broken callback must not corrupt the element's state or abort the rest of a
coordinated update, and there is nothing useful this can do about it besides
make it visible.
